gaps.fact: Knights Valley is a Sonoma County AVA, the warmest in Sonoma, though it sits beside Calistoga: the article names it in places and card 3, and a producer record notes the trap, but no chapter names it and no question asks which county it is in.
The Napa River running south into San Pablo Bay, and the Sonoma Mountains as a range: both stand in the article's terroir only; neither chapter names them and no question asks them.

A named single vineyard needs 95 per cent of its fruit from that vineyard: taught only in the central-coast article (law, labels; trap 7) and the explanation of a region question; no chapter states it and no question of either bank asks it.

Claret as an American label term, one of the semi-generic names kept only on labels approved before the 2006 accord with the European Union: the banks ask Claret only as English trade usage for red Bordeaux (i-hujyk668) and ask the grandfather clause only for Champagne (c-e0xdtz3u).
Beringer, St Helena, 1876, the valley's longest unbroken run through Prohibition: it has an article and a producer record but appears in the banks only as a distractor (i-rujlnvtp).
Six of the Court's names appear nowhere in the Codex: Far Niente, Groth, Etude, Quintessa, Merryvale and Larkmead.

Spottswoode, Cakebread, Silver Oak, Chappellet, Caymus, Iron Horse, Williams Selyem and Kistler are taught only in the article's producer list (Silver Oak also in region question r-ycjji2uf); no chapter names them and no question of either bank asks any of them.
The quality of the last five North Coast vintages: nothing in the Codex covers it. It is volatile by nature, so it belongs in a dated note refreshed each year, not in a question.

Agoston Haraszthy, founder of Buena Vista at Sonoma in 1857 and the importer of European cuttings: he is never named; the article's Buena Vista line says only a Hungarian count, and his name appears in the banks only as a distractor (i-ba0qgwkg).

Warren Winiarski, who founded Stag's Leap Wine Cellars and made its winning 1973 Cabernet, appears only in one producer record's holdings line; Charles Krug, Napa's oldest winery of 1861, only in the article; neither is in a chapter or asked in either bank.

errors.where: js/regions/california.json, records.california.labels (Vintage): "a wine whose only origin is American carries no vintage"; the same record's ladder (American): "it may carry no vintage"
errors.claim: A wine whose appellation is American, the country, may not carry a vintage date.
errors.correction: The Village bank teaches the opposite in c-il084y1r: since a federal rule that took effect late in 2012 an American wine may carry a vintage when 85 per cent of it comes from that harvest, the figure 27 CFR 4.27(a) now asks for any appellation other than an AVA. The country article and the Village question cannot both stand; the two article lines should follow the question, after a check of the current text of 4.27.
errors.source: 27 CFR 4.27(a), Vintage wine; the Codex's own c-il084y1r

courtUpdates.printed: Napa County: Mount Veeder AVA, Calistoga AVA, Yountville AVA
courtUpdates.now: The Calistoga AVA's boundary was modified by the same rule that established Crystal Springs of Napa Valley, the seventeenth AVA nested in Napa Valley, both effective 15 November 2024; Calistoga lost a sliver to avoid a partial overlap. The napa-sonoma article already carries both (Calistoga trimmed 2024; Crystal Springs, card 8).

notes: Mapped questions: Régionale 61 (United States: 16 North Coast stems, 17 on California at large and on federal law, 4 Central Coast, 2 Central Valley and Sierra Foothills, 13 Oregon and Washington, 5 New York, 4 other states) and Village 40 (California: 21 North Coast, 3 on state and federal labelling, 12 Central Coast, 4 Lodi and the Sierra Foothills), 101 in all; a further 14 North Coast stems sit outside the map in Producers & Icons, History & Figures, Sparkling Wine World, Geography & Maps, Grapes & Labels and Classifications & Labels and are cited in the coverage. The subject is well taught where the exam leans: the Napa and Sonoma AVAs and their grapes, the Mayacamas and the Vaca, the bay and the Petaluma Gap, the soils from Goldridge to Howell Mountain's red earth, the label percentages, Estate Bottled, Meritage, Reserve and the Paris tasting. The thin cells are the producers (six of the Court's names are absent and eight more live only in the article), Knights Valley, Claret on an American label, the single vineyard 95 per cent, Haraszthy, Winiarski and Charles Krug, and the vintage row, which nothing covers. One error, at medium confidence: the california country record says an American wine may carry no vintage, against the Village question c-il084y1r. Checked and sound: the calnorth chapter's percentages, including vintage at 95 per cent with an AVA and 85 otherwise and wholly Californian fruit under any California or county name; Tchelistcheff at Beaulieu in 1938; the AXR1 parentage; Heitz's Martha's Vineyard from 1966; the Paris pair of 1973. The Court's own Estate Bottled cell says the fruit must be in the same county; the federal rule is the same AVA as the winery, which is what the Codex teaches, and the Court's text stands as printed. For the owner, a house rule rather than a fact: c-t8931nxl (California, the Paris tasting of the History & Lore row) offers a living wine writer as one of its three distractors; its facts are sound. One search spent, on the Calistoga boundary, which found the 2024 modification logged above; the second was not needed.
